title: Acne Vulgaris: Severity, Scarring Risk, and Antibiotic Stewardship
bottomLine: Acne treatment is severity- and scar-risk based. Use topical retinoid/benzoyl-peroxide based therapy for most patients, reserve systemic antibiotics for appropriate inflammatory disease with benzoyl peroxide, reassess by about 3 months, and escalate early when scarring or major psychosocial harm is occurring.
recognize: Comedones support acne vulgaris; inflammatory papules/pustules/nodules determine severity and scar risk.
Jawline/cyclic disease may have an androgen-responsive component.
differentiate: Rosacea lacks comedones and is centrofacial; folliculitis, perioral dermatitis and drug eruptions can mimic acne.
assessment: Assess distribution, nodules/scars, prior treatment/adherence, pregnancy potential, medications/supplements and mental-health impact.
workup: Typical acne is a clinical diagnosis; endocrine testing is targeted to hyperandrogenism/irregular menses or another clinical indication rather than routine.
management: Use topical retinoid and/or benzoyl peroxide based regimens for comedonal/mild inflammatory disease; add systemic therapy for moderate-severe disease according to current Canadian guidance.
Oral antibiotics should be time-limited and combined with benzoyl peroxide; severe nodulocystic/scarring disease warrants isotretinoin-capable specialist management.
medicationSafety: Avoid topical/oral retinoids in pregnancy; isotretinoin requires strict pregnancy-prevention/monitoring requirements.
Do not use prolonged antibiotic monotherapy because resistance and microbiome harm increase.
redFlags: Major depressive/suicidal symptoms related to disease or treatment
Pregnancy with teratogenic acne medication exposure
counselling: Apply topical therapy to the acne-prone area, not only individual lesions; expect improvement over weeks, not days.
followUp: Reassess efficacy/tolerance after an adequate trial and oral-antibiotic need by about 3 months.
examTrap: Continuing an oral antibiotic indefinitely because acne is somewhat improved instead of reassessing and transitioning to a sustainable regimen.
oneLinePearl: Acne therapy should prevent scars without creating antibiotic dependence.

title: Rosacea: Phenotype the Face Before Treating It Like Acne
bottomLine: Rosacea is a chronic centrofacial inflammatory/vascular disorder. Identify erythematotelangiectatic, papulopustular, phymatous and ocular features, avoid acne-style comedonal assumptions, and treat the dominant phenotype while protecting the eyes when ocular disease is present.
recognize: Persistent centrofacial erythema, flushing, telangiectasia and inflammatory papules/pustules occur without true comedones.
Ocular rosacea can cause gritty/burning eyes, blepharitis or keratitis.
differentiate: Acne has comedones; seborrheic dermatitis has greasy scale; lupus/photosensitive eruptions and perioral dermatitis require different pathways.
assessment: Assess triggers, ocular symptoms, skin-care irritants, steroid exposure and phymatous change.
workup: Typical rosacea is clinical; investigate autoimmune/infectious mimics only when the pattern is atypical.
management: Use gentle skin care, sun protection and trigger reduction; topical anti-inflammatory/vasoconstrictive options and oral tetracycline-class anti-inflammatory therapy are selected by phenotype/severity.
Ocular symptoms require lid hygiene and ophthalmic evaluation when pain, photophobia or visual change is present.
medicationSafety: Avoid chronic topical corticosteroids on facial rosacea because rebound/periorificial disease can worsen.
redFlags: Atypical fixed rash with systemic autoimmune features
counselling: Explain that flushing triggers vary and total trigger avoidance is neither realistic nor required for effective care.
followUp: Reassess dominant phenotype, ocular symptoms and medication tolerability.
examTrap: Treating papulopustular rosacea as acne with comedone-focused therapy while missing ocular disease.
oneLinePearl: No comedones plus centrofacial flushing should make you think rosacea, not acne.

title: Atopic Dermatitis: Repair the Barrier, Control Inflammation, Watch for Infection
bottomLine: Atopic dermatitis is chronic relapsing pruritic eczema. Daily barrier care plus appropriately potent anti-inflammatory therapy is the foundation; persistent disease requires trigger/adherence review and step-up therapy, while eczema herpeticum or serious bacterial superinfection is urgent.
recognize: Pruritus, xerosis and age-patterned eczematous plaques support the diagnosis.
Skin of colour may show gray-brown/violet inflammation rather than bright erythema.
differentiate: Contact dermatitis is exposure-pattern driven; scabies causes characteristic distribution/contacts; psoriasis has sharper plaques and different scale patterns.
assessment: Assess sleep, itch, infection, treatment amount/technique, irritant/fragrance exposure, asthma/allergic disease and quality-of-life burden.
workup: Typical disease is clinical; allergy testing is not routine unless history suggests a specific immediate food allergy or contact trigger; patch testing is used for suspected allergic contact dermatitis.
management: Use regular emollients and short courses/maintenance strategies with topical corticosteroids of site-appropriate potency or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agents.
Moderate-severe refractory disease warrants phototherapy/systemic/biologic specialty pathways.
medicationSafety: Match topical steroid potency and duration to body site/age; avoid steroid phobia that leads to undertreatment while also avoiding chronic high-potency use on thin skin.
Topical calcineurin inhibitors remain useful steroid-sparing therapy for appropriate sites.
redFlags: Painful monomorphic vesicles/erosions suggesting eczema herpeticum
Severe sleep/feeding impairment in a child
counselling: Use fragrance-free gentle skin care and explain proactive maintenance for recurrent sites rather than only rescue treatment.
followUp: Reassess control, infections, steroid exposure and need for escalation.
examTrap: Ordering broad food-allergy panels for eczema without an immediate-reaction history.
oneLinePearl: Eczema control is barrier repair plus enough anti-inflammatory treatment to actually suppress the flare.

title: Contact Dermatitis: Irritant or Allergic? Map the Exposure
bottomLine: Contact dermatitis diagnosis depends on morphology plus exposure pattern. Irritant disease is direct barrier injury; allergic disease is delayed hypersensitivity. Remove the culprit, repair the barrier and treat inflammation; use patch testing when allergic contact dermatitis remains plausible or recurrent.
recognize: Irritant dermatitis often affects hands/wet-work sites and may burn/fissure; allergic dermatitis can spread beyond exact contact borders and recur with small exposures.
differentiate: Atopic dermatitis, tinea, psoriasis, scabies and cellulitis can mimic contact dermatitis.
assessment: Build a detailed home/work/hobby/product timeline including soaps, gloves, adhesives, metals, fragrances, preservatives, plants and topical medications.
workup: Patch testing diagnoses delayed allergic contact dermatitis; prick/IgE testing does not substitute for patch testing.
management: Eliminate/substitute the exposure, use barrier protection/emollients and site-appropriate topical anti-inflammatory therapy.
Occupational disease may require modified duties and occupational-health coordination.
medicationSafety: Topical antibiotics themselves can cause allergic contact dermatitis; routine use on uncomplicated wounds should be avoided.
redFlags: Facial/airway swelling suggesting immediate allergy rather than dermatitis
counselling: Teach label/allergen-name review because the same allergen may appear in multiple products.
followUp: Persistent/recurrent disease despite avoidance warrants dermatology/patch testing.
examTrap: Ordering serum allergy testing for a delayed eczematous rash caused by nickel or preservative exposure.
oneLinePearl: Contact dermatitis is solved by the exposure map, not a generic allergy panel.
sourceBasis: Canadian Dermatology Association eczema/contact dermatitis resources

title: Psoriasis: Skin Disease With Joint and Cardiometabolic Consequences
bottomLine: Psoriasis is chronic immune-mediated disease, not only a rash. Confirm the phenotype, screen for psoriatic arthritis and psychosocial/cardiometabolic burden, use topical therapy for limited disease, and escalate moderate-severe or joint disease to systemic/biologic pathways.
recognize: Well-demarcated plaques with scale on extensor/scalp/sacral sites are typical; inverse, guttate, pustular and erythrodermic variants differ.
Joint pain, morning stiffness, dactylitis or enthesitis can signal psoriatic arthritis.
differentiate: Tinea can mimic plaques and worsens with inappropriate steroid-only therapy; seborrheic dermatitis is greasier/less sharply demarcated.
assessment: Assess extent/site, nails, joints, obesity/metabolic risk, smoking/alcohol, mood, pregnancy and previous systemic therapy.
workup: Diagnosis is usually clinical; biopsy is reserved for uncertainty; systemic-treatment screening/labs are drug-specific.
management: Topical corticosteroid/vitamin-D or other nonsteroidal agents are used for limited disease; phototherapy/systemic/biologic therapy is appropriate for substantial extent, high-impact sites or psoriatic arthritis.
medicationSafety: Systemic immunomodulators require infection/vaccination and drug-specific laboratory monitoring.
Avoid abrupt systemic corticosteroid use as routine psoriasis therapy because rebound/pustular disease can occur.
redFlags: Generalized pustular psoriasis with systemic illness
counselling: Address cardiovascular risk and stigma as part of disease care, not as unrelated issues.
followUp: Track skin/joint response and treatment toxicity; escalate uncontrolled high-impact disease.
examTrap: Treating plaques while never asking about inflammatory joint symptoms.
oneLinePearl: Psoriasis can damage joints and cardiometabolic health even when the rash is the visible problem.

title: Seborrheic Dermatitis: Control Yeast-Associated Inflammation, Not Just Scale
bottomLine: Seborrheic dermatitis is chronic relapsing inflammation in sebum-rich areas. Use antifungal therapy plus short anti-inflammatory courses when needed, then maintenance; severe new-onset/refractory disease should prompt review for immunosuppression or neurologic comorbidity rather than endless steroid use.
recognize: Greasy scale/erythema on scalp, eyebrows, nasolabial folds, ears and chest are typical.
differentiate: Psoriasis has thicker sharply demarcated plaques; tinea capitis may cause alopecia/broken hairs; atopic dermatitis has different distribution/history.
assessment: Assess distribution, infant vs adult pattern, HIV/immunosuppression risk when unusually severe, and prior steroid/antifungal use.
workup: Typical disease is clinical; fungal testing or biopsy is used only when a mimic is plausible.
management: Use ketoconazole/other antifungal shampoo or topical antifungal and brief low-potency anti-inflammatory therapy on sensitive sites; maintenance antifungal use reduces relapse.
medicationSafety: Avoid chronic potent topical steroids on face/folds because atrophy, telangiectasia and periorificial dermatitis can occur.
redFlags: Severe diffuse disease with immunosuppression concern
counselling: Explain the relapsing nature so maintenance is expected rather than interpreted as treatment failure.
followUp: Reassess refractory/atypical disease for psoriasis, tinea or systemic risk.
examTrap: Using potent facial steroids indefinitely for recurrent scale without antifungal maintenance or diagnosis review.
oneLinePearl: Seborrheic dermatitis is controlled, not cured; antifungal maintenance matters.
sourceBasis: Canadian Dermatology Association seborrheic dermatitis resources

title: Bacterial Skin Infections: Cellulitis, Abscess, or Pseudocellulitis?
bottomLine: Skin infection treatment starts by naming the syndrome. Cellulitis is usually unilateral spreading dermal infection; abscess needs drainage/source control; bilateral lower-leg erythema often represents pseudocellulitis. Escalate systemic toxicity, rapidly progressive pain or necrotizing features immediately.
recognize: Cellulitis causes warmth/tenderness/spreading erythema; abscess causes a fluctuant purulent collection; impetigo produces superficial crusted lesions.
differentiate: Stasis dermatitis, lipodermatosclerosis, lymphedema, gout, contact dermatitis and tinea commonly mimic cellulitis, especially when both legs are involved.
assessment: Assess vitals/toxicity, pain severity, rapidity, purulence, trauma/bite, edema, diabetes/immunosuppression, water exposure and recurrent infection.
workup: Cultures are most useful for purulent drainage, severe/atypical infection or treatment failure; uncomplicated cellulitis is usually clinical.
management: Drain uncomplicated abscesses; add antibiotics when systemic illness, extensive cellulitis, immunocompromise or other high-risk features justify them.
Use syndrome/local-resistance appropriate antibiotics and reassess failure rather than automatically broadening therapy.
medicationSafety: Avoid routine antibiotics for bilateral lower-leg redness without a convincing infection syndrome.
Avoid routine topical antibiotics on clean dermatologic wounds because contact allergy/resistance can outweigh benefit.
counselling: Mark/monitor progression when useful and give return precautions for spread, fever, severe pain or systemic symptoms.
followUp: Reassess within an appropriate interval when severity/risk warrants; recurrent cellulitis requires edema/skin-barrier/tinea review.
examTrap: Prescribing antibiotics for bilateral chronic red swollen legs without considering stasis dermatitis.
oneLinePearl: Before treating cellulitis, ask whether it is unilateral infection, a drainable abscess, or pseudocellulitis.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Emergency Medicine recommendations

title: Viral Skin Infections: Localized Disease or High-Risk Dissemination?
bottomLine: Most viral skin infections are diagnosed clinically, but immune status, pregnancy, eye involvement, dissemination and pain pattern determine urgency. Distinguish HSV, zoster, warts and molluscum from bacterial/fungal mimics and use antiviral therapy when timing/severity/risk supports it.
recognize: HSV often causes grouped painful vesicles/erosions; zoster follows a dermatomal painful vesicular eruption; warts are papillomatous; molluscum has umbilicated papules.
differentiate: Impetigo can crust after vesicles rupture; contact dermatitis can blister; eczema herpeticum is disseminated HSV on eczematous skin and is urgent.
assessment: Assess onset, pain, distribution, eye/ear involvement, pregnancy, immune status, newborn exposure and neurologic symptoms.
workup: Swab HSV/VZV lesions when confirmation changes management, especially atypical, disseminated or pregnancy/neonatal contexts; typical warts/molluscum rarely need testing.
management: Use oral antiviral therapy for indicated HSV/zoster presentations and urgent specialty/acute-care management for disseminated, ophthalmic, neurologic or severe immunocompromised disease.
Warts/molluscum can be observed or treated based on symptoms/location/immunocompromise.
medicationSafety: Renal function matters for systemic acyclovir/valacyclovir dosing; dehydration increases toxicity risk.
counselling: Explain transmission precautions and that zoster vaccine is preventive rather than treatment of an active eruption.
followUp: Reassess eye/neurologic symptoms, persistent pain or immunocompromised disease promptly.
examTrap: Treating vesicles around the eye as routine dermatitis instead of considering HSV/zoster ophthalmic disease.
oneLinePearl: Viral skin disease becomes urgent when it reaches the eye, nervous system, newborn or immunocompromised host.
sourceBasis: Canadian Dermatology Association viral skin condition resources

title: Fungal Skin Infections: Confirm the Pattern Before Systemic Therapy
bottomLine: Dermatophyte infection is a clinical-pattern diagnosis that should be confirmed when uncertain or before systemic nail therapy. Use topical therapy for limited skin disease, systemic therapy for appropriate scalp/extensive/nail disease, and avoid antifungal–steroid combination misuse that masks tinea.
recognize: Tinea corporis often has annular scale with an advancing edge; tinea pedis/intertrigo patterns vary; tinea capitis can cause scale, broken hairs or inflammatory kerion.
differentiate: Eczema, psoriasis and contact dermatitis can mimic tinea; onychomycosis accounts for only a portion of dystrophic nails.
assessment: Assess site/extent, scalp/nails, diabetes/immunosuppression, household/animal exposure, prior steroid use and pregnancy/liver disease before systemic treatment.
workup: Use KOH/culture or other mycologic confirmation when morphology is uncertain and before systemic onychomycosis treatment; tinea capitis often warrants organism-aware confirmation according to local practice.
management: Use topical antifungal therapy for limited skin disease; scalp and selected extensive/refractory/nail disease require systemic agents with organism/site and patient factors considered.
medicationSafety: Do not prescribe systemic antifungals for suspected onychomycosis without mycological confirmation.
Avoid fixed potent steroid–antifungal combinations that can produce tinea incognito and treatment failure; systemic azoles/terbinafine have hepatic/drug-interaction considerations.
redFlags: Kerion with risk of scarring alopecia
counselling: Treat affected contacts/environment when indicated and keep feet/groin folds dry; explain why nail confirmation matters before months of systemic therapy.
followUp: Reassess persistent disease for incorrect diagnosis, reinfection, resistance/adherence or immunosuppression.
examTrap: Prescribing oral terbinafine for a thick dystrophic nail without confirming fungal infection.
oneLinePearl: If systemic antifungal treatment carries months of risk, prove the fungus first.
sourceBasis: Canadian Dermatology Association fungal skin condition resources
